To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) CFTR is expressed in cholangiocyte cells, (2) SULT1E 1 is expressed in hepatic cells, (3) CFTR is not expressed in hepatic cell and, (4) SULT1EI is induced by a paracrinemechanism in the absence of CF TR in cholangiocyctes.
CFTR-deficiency induces SULT1 E1 expression in hepatocyes and alters the activity of estrogenic pathways.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a membrane separated cholangiocyte/human hepatocyte co-cultured system to determine the mechanism by which loss of CFTR function in cholangiocyte cells stimulates SULT1E
the development of CFTR-targeting drugs for CF lung disease and CFTR-independent drugs for CF liver disease.
understanding the mechanism of liver disease in CF.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CFTR deficiency in cholangiocyte cells induces SULT1A1 expression in hepatocyte cells via paracrine signaling.
the absence of CF in the bile duct epithelium stimulates the expression of the estrogen sulfotransferases (SULT1E1) in hepatocytes by an unknown mechanism.
the loss of CF transmembrane conductive regulator (CFTR), which is expressed only in cholangiocyte cells, stimulates the expression of the sulfotransferases in hepatocytes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the lack of CFTR in cholangiocyte cells stimulates the paracrine expression of SULT 1E1 in adjacent hepatocytes.
CFTR loss in cholangiocyte cells stimulates SULT1E2 activity in hepatocytes via paracrine signaling, which in turn alters the expression of E2 regulated genes in hepatocytes.
the absence of CF transmembrane regulator (CFTR, a chloride channel) in cholangiocyte cells induces sulfotransferases in hepatocytes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SULT1A1 and SULT1E are the two main SULTs in the liver.
